meta.title: Home | Green Ecolution | Smart Green Space Management
meta.description: Green Ecolution enables smart irrigation of green spaces through sensor-based monitoring and data-driven recommendations.

hero.description: Sensor-based monitoring of green spaces transmits data over the LoRaWAN network for analysis, so that irrigation recommendations can be provided.

moisture.label: Measuring irrigation status
moisture.description: Soil moisture is measured at different soil depths depending on the vegetation type, providing data across different soil layers.

transmission.label: Data transmission
transmission.description: The sensor data is transmitted via a public LoRaWAN network to a backend for further processing. LoRaWAN requires little energy and has a long range, resulting in wide area coverage and low maintenance effort.

recommendation.label: Recommendations
recommendation.description: The transmitted sensor data is analyzed using scientific and mathematical methods. A dashboard graphically shows whether irrigation will be needed soon. <Link>See the benefits</Link>

welcomeCard.description: Learn how we use smart sensors and data-driven analysis to optimize the irrigation of urban green spaces, for healthier trees, beds and parks with efficient use of resources.

adoptModal.waitingIn: is waiting for you in Flensburg
adoptModal.quote: “Thank you for thinking of me! With projects like Green Ecolution, city trees like me finally get the attention we deserve.”

facts.evaporation: A large city tree can evaporate up to 400 liters of water a day, cooling its surroundings by up to 3°C.
facts.oxygen: A single beech tree produces enough oxygen for 10 people per year.
facts.dust: City trees filter a significant share of particulate matter from the air in their immediate surroundings.
facts.roots: The roots of a street tree often extend over one and a half times the area of its crown.
facts.co2: Over its lifetime, a 100-year-old tree has bound around 5 tons of CO₂.
facts.network: Trees communicate through underground fungal networks, known as the “Wood Wide Web”.
facts.lifespan: Street trees live an average of only 60 years. In rural areas, they live three times as long.
facts.noise: A dense stand of trees can reduce noise levels by up to 10 decibels.
facts.water: In hot summers, a city tree needs up to 200 additional liters of water per week.

introduction.title: What does smart green space management involve?
introduction.description: In smart green space management, sensors continuously monitor green spaces and provide the data basis for their irrigation and care. This allows measures to be controlled precisely and adapted to the respective site conditions.

sensor.label: Development of a sensor solution
sensor.description: Soil moisture data is provided by sensors placed at different depths.

evaluation.label: Analysis of measurement data
evaluation.description: Analysis of the data transmitted by sensors for demand-based irrigation of young trees.

youngTrees.label: Focus on young trees
youngTrees.description: Young trees are particularly vulnerable to heat and therefore need protection. That's why trees are monitored during their first three years at their site.

monitoring.label: Monitoring multiple locations
monitoring.description: Using the LoRaWAN network, different locations can be monitored, and additional ones can easily be added.

challenge.supportingText: Urban green spaces regulate the microclimate, promote biodiversity and strengthen a location's competitiveness. But persistent drought and a lack of digitalization threaten this asset. Many municipalities base their irrigation planning solely on the judgment of individual staff, with no data basis at all. Instead of demand-based irrigation, watering is done uniformly, wasting water while still not reaching every tree. Unoptimized irrigation trips also cause avoidable CO₂ emissions.

waterUse.description: Water is consumed by a mid-sized municipality for irrigation, often without a data basis and without demand-based control.

treeCost.description: is the cost of a single street tree. If it is lost due to insufficient irrigation, this damage alone covers the sensor costs for several years.

bedCost.description: can be the cost of a complete street bed, including civil works, substrate and infrastructure.

targetGroups.title: Who benefits
targetGroups.description: Green Ecolution is built for municipal operations. The benefit differs depending on the role.

municipality.description: Decisions about water, staff and vehicles rest on measurements instead of experience. Consumption and operations are documented per area and per tour, and can therefore be evidenced.

operations.description: Schedules and tours are generated instead of assembled by hand. The fleet, the teams and the review of actual consumption all live in one place.

field.description: The tour can be viewed in the app and can also be transferred to the navigation device in the vehicle. A traffic-light system on the map shows which trees and groups need water.

it.description: The platform runs in a Kubernetes cluster, in your own or the municipality's infrastructure, or hosted. Open interfaces and a plug-in system keep the data within your own reach.

targetGroups.closing: Everyone else benefits indirectly: healthy urban trees cool the city climate and support biodiversity.

sensorProbe.illustrationAriaLabel: Schematic diagram of a soil probe at three depths
sensorProbe.title: The soil probe
sensorProbe.description: Designed for use in public spaces. Sensors at three depths (30, 60 and 90 cm) capture the full root profile of a tree, from the near-surface fine roots to the deeper main roots. This makes it possible to see whether water actually reaches the root zone or only wets the surface. Installation is flush with the ground using standard soil augers. Maintenance work such as mowing is not affected.
sensorProbe.probeCarrier: The probe is the carrier, not the sensor. It takes several sensor types, so the configuration can be matched to the requirements.
sensorProbe.availability: The probes are available through PROGEEK GmbH.

measure.title: Measure
measure.description: Soil moisture sensors capture parameters such as soil moisture, temperature, and soil water tension at multiple depths (30/60/90 cm). The data is transmitted energy-efficiently via LoRaWAN.

understand.title: Understand
understand.description: A traffic-light system shows the current irrigation need on a map. Staff can see at a glance which green spaces need water. Time series enable detailed analyses.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about Green Ecolution

origin.question: Who is behind the Green Ecolution project?
origin.answerPlain:
Green Ecolution started out as a master's project in Applied Computer Science at Flensburg University of Applied Sciences, together with the municipal service centre of Flensburg and Smarte Grenzregion. The question was whether watering in municipal day-to-day work can really be steered by data, with sensors in the soil and tours derived from them.

The answer was clear. In user tests with the service centre the application scored an above-average usability rating and was described as clear and manageable even by staff without an IT background.

On that foundation PROGEEK is building the solution municipalities can use today. Sensors and platform have been laid out for regular operation.

value.question: What value does the project provide?
value.answerPlain:
Green Ecolution makes the watering of urban trees traceable. Sensor data shows which areas need water, and the scheduling turns that into tours without unnecessary trips. This lowers water consumption and maintenance effort and puts decisions on measurements instead of experience.

For municipalities that means missing water becomes visible earlier, consumption is documented, and the solution can be operated in-house and developed further together, without being tied to a single vendor.

requirements.question: What does a municipality need to bring?
requirements.answerPlain:
For scheduling and route planning, the locations of the trees and areas, the vehicles you already have with their water capacities and the refill points across the city are enough. Sensors are not a prerequisite for this; they improve the prioritisation. Once probes are added, LoRaWAN coverage is needed.

Which data and which infrastructure are needed in detail is set out under the requirements on the project page.

openSource.question: What does it mean that the project is publicly accessible?
openSource.answerPlain:
The project's source code is available in a publicly accessible GitHub repository. This means the current state of development can be viewed at any time, which creates transparency and allows interested people to follow the ongoing development or get actively involved.

A connection to the Open Data Portal of the state of Schleswig-Holstein is also planned for the future, in order to make selected sensor data publicly accessible. This extension is currently in the planning stage.

sensors.question: Does the system only work with the sensors you mention?
sensors.answerPlain:
The soil probe is our own development, designed for use in public spaces. It is the carrier, and it takes several sensor types at up to three depths, which makes it possible to cover the root profile of a tree.

The tested configuration combines a Watermark sensor for soil water tension with an SMT100 sensor for soil moisture and temperature. That combination is a deliberate choice: only tension together with volumetric moisture and temperature gives a reliable picture of how much water is actually available to the tree.

Other LoRaWAN soil moisture sensors can be connected through The Things Network and the plug-in system. This has not been tested in the field so far.

progress.question: What is the current progress of the project?
progress.answerPlain:
The "Green Ecolution" research project was successfully completed as part of the Applied Computer Science (Angewandte Informatik) master's program at Hochschule Flensburg. Building on the results achieved in the project, the further development is now being continued.

In October 2025, the project received funding through the DigitalHub Call for Concepts of the state program "Offene Innovation – Open Source made in Schleswig-Holstein." This enables the system to be further expanded and tested in practice.

PROGEEK, the City of Flensburg, and Smarte Grenzregion are currently working together on the further development and integration of the system, in order to transfer the insights gained into everyday municipal practice on a lasting basis.
